books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the account of the Maine Law of 1851 and the temperance movement in the course books. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In 1851, Maine became the first state to ban the manufacture and sale of alcoholic drinks. The law, pushed by the temperance movement and its leader Neal Dow, aimed to protect families from the harm reformers blamed on drinking. Within a few years, a dozen other states passed similar laws.

rationales.A: Background from the books: temperance leaders were mostly native-born Protestants; the immigrants were the people their campaigns targeted, not the leaders.
rationales.B: Temperance laws banned drink, not people; the overlap was over drinking habits, not over closing the ports.
rationales.C: Background from the books: native-born reformers saw Irish pubs and German beer halls as proof that immigrants lacked self-control, and temperance became one more way to press newcomers to change.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Know-Nothings fought immigrants, not for slavery; temperance and nativism met over drink, not over slavery’s spread.
rationales.general:
1. Ask whom temperance reformers watched: immigrant neighborhoods, their pubs and beer halls.
2. Background from the books: nativists read immigrant drinking as a lack of the self-control proper middle-class Protestants prized.
3. See the overlap: one movement’s moral cause became the other’s weapon against newcomers.
Remember: two movements overlap where they name the same enemy; find the shared target.
